title: Green Renovation and Construction
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss green renovation versus demolition and greener construction. They open with the hundred-mile food movement and J.B. McKinnon's idea of "vertical agitation" for picking one environmental cause. They cover construction and demolition waste (about 136 million tons in 2007, 142 million tons in 2010, with most now recycled), why renovating is usually greener than tearing down, deconstructing a house by hand (EPA-rated reuse of 70 to 90 percent), ReStore salvage stores, Craigslist giveaways, on-site pulverizing of demolition waste, and green materials such as recycled laminate, bamboo, cork, recycled glass countertops, and tankless water heaters. They also cover insulation (fiberglass concerns versus recycled denim and newspaper), compact fluorescent bulbs, and the World Trade Center steel recycling. The episode ends with listener mail and movie recommendations.

segments.title: Opening banter and the hundred-mile food movement
segments.summary: The hosts joke about their outfits, then discuss J.B. McKinnon, the hundred-mile food movement, and his idea of vertical agitation, which means picking one environmental cause and focusing on it, drawing on Stanley Cohen's book States of Denial.

segments.title: Construction and demolition waste and reducing the waste stream
segments.summary: The hosts describe construction and demolition waste as one of the largest sectors of municipal waste. They mention a carpet company that leases carpeting and takes it back for recycling. They also explain the reduce, reuse, recycle hierarchy and note that recycling still has costs such as trucks and fuel.

segments.title: Renovating versus demolishing
segments.summary: The hosts argue that renovating is generally greener than full demolition because it produces less waste and saves the foundation and studs. They cite figures of about 136 million tons of construction and demolition waste in 2007 and 142 million tons in 2010, with a large share now recycled.

segments.title: ReStore salvage stores and hand deconstruction
segments.summary: The hosts describe ReStore as a nonprofit that sells salvaged doors, windows, and fixtures. In Seattle, ReStore demolishes houses by hand and recycles nearly everything, earning EPA reuse ratings of 70 to 90 percent and a tax deduction for donors. Hand demolition also protects tree roots and underground utilities.

segments.title: Disposing of demolition materials
segments.summary: The hosts suggest giving away unwanted materials on Craigslist, where people often take bricks and doors for free. They describe a company that pulverizes demolition waste on site, separates the nails, and uses the crushed material as driveway base. They also warn that DIY demolition can be dangerous and cost about ten thousand dollars to save.

segments.title: Green building materials
segments.summary: The hosts discuss recycled building materials, including post-industrial and post-consumer content, fly ash in concrete, recycled laminate flooring, and composite decking made from recycled plastic bottles. They also cover bamboo flooring, which is a fast-growing grass, cork flooring, and the sustainability of these materials.

segments.title: Tankless water heaters, insulation, and countertops
segments.summary: The hosts explain that tankless on-demand water heaters avoid keeping a large tank hot, and that payback depends on how long you stay in the house. They then discuss insulation, noting fiberglass health concerns and the alternative of recycled denim and newspaper. Recycled paper, glass, and aluminum countertops are also mentioned.

segments.title: Compact fluorescent bulbs and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the controversy over compact fluorescent bulbs, including their cool light and their longer life, and estimate the energy and greenhouse gas savings if every household swapped one bulb. They then wrap up the green construction topic and point listeners to HowStuffWorks green content.

segments.title: Listener mail and movie recommendations
segments.summary: The hosts read a listener email about the Snuggie inventor's daughter's party, then go through listener suggestions for overlooked movies, including Attack the Gas Station, Office Space, Idiocracy, The Proposition, Sunshine, and Synecdoche, New York.
